Study Abstract

Background. EHR data from community-based naturopathic clinics are a largely untapped resource for health services research. Prior studies relied on billing data, which do not capture the clinical narrative documentation central to naturopathic care — including supplement recommendations, lifestyle counseling, and integrative treatment rationale.

Purpose. To establish and validate a privacy-first, cloud-based informatics pipeline for multi-clinic naturopathic EHR data, and to demonstrate its analytic utility through glycemic cohort analysis and treatment pattern characterization.

Methods. FHIR APIs were used to ingest structured and unstructured EHR data from seven CharmHealth-based naturopathic clinics in Washington State into Google Cloud Platform (GCP) under a HIPAA BAA. De-identification was performed using the GCP Healthcare De-identification API, supplemented by a custom 9-pass rule-based NLP redaction pipeline verified by manual safety audit. De-identified clinical notes (n=858,394) were converted into a structured treatment table using rule-based keyword NLP (13 categories; PPV 97.9%) and loaded into BigQuery.

Results. The database contains 58,498 patients, 469,162 encounters, and 3.8 million observations across 7 clinics (2012–2026); 67.5% female, mean age 42.6 years. The most common conditions were fatigue, insomnia, anxiety, hyperlipidemia, and constipation. Treatment pattern analysis (n=43,747 note patients) showed supplement/botanical recommendations in 61.6% of patients, followed by lab/diagnostic orders (35.4%), diet/nutrition counseling (30.5%), and referrals (25.8%). A glycemic cohort (HbA1c-defined, not diagnosis codes) included diabetes (≥6.5%, n=355), prediabetes (5.7–6.4%, n=2,254), and normoglycemic (<5.7%, n=10,127) patients. In the longitudinal subset (≥2 readings), the diabetes group showed a mean HbA1c reduction of −0.766% (7.97% → 7.21%; p<0.001; mean follow-up 671 days); the prediabetes group showed −0.131% (5.87% → 5.74%; p<0.001; 684 days), with durable stabilization maintained through 24+ months.

Conclusions. This pilot demonstrates that a scalable, HIPAA-compliant, cloud-native infrastructure can transform naturopathic EHR data — including free-text clinical narrative — into a structured research dataset supporting longitudinal and treatment pattern analyses. The glycemic findings support the feasibility of future comparative effectiveness research using naturopathic EHR data at scale.

HbA1c Cohort Analysis
HbA1c-threshold cohort  •  7 naturopathic clinics  •  Rule-based NLP treatment extraction (PPV 97.9%)  •  Paired t-test longitudinal HbA1c outcomes
Two cohorts are used in this section:
  • Treatment cohort (n=3,149): all patients with any HbA1c ≥5.7% (prediabetes or diabetes range at first reading). Used for all treatment frequency tables.
  • Longitudinal outcomes cohort (n=1,581): all patients with ≥2 HbA1c readings on distinct dates, regardless of baseline value. Used for HbA1c change analyses. Includes 1,581 elevated-baseline patients (diabetes n=238, prediabetes n=1,343) plus 3,992 normoglycemic patients as an internal comparator group.

HbA1c Cohort Analysis: Treatment × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

What is a linear mixed effects model?
A linear mixed effects (LME) model is designed for data where the same individuals are measured repeatedly over time. Rather than treating each HbA1c reading as independent, it estimates a shared population-level trajectory while allowing each patient to start at their own personal baseline level (the “random intercept”). Treatment × time interaction terms then ask: do patients with documented receipt of a given treatment show a systematically faster or slower rate of HbA1c change compared to patients without that treatment, after adjusting for covariates? The coefficient β/yr is the additional annual HbA1c change associated with each treatment, relative to the reference slope.

Model & Cohort

Outcome: HbA1c at each visit. Fixed effects: time, baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication, clinic. Random intercept per patient. 10 treatment categories tested simultaneously (Bonferroni threshold: p = 0.0045). Cohort: n=622 patients, 1,975 observations; median follow-up 400 days; ICC = 0.25 (confirms within-patient clustering warrants mixed model). Reference slope (no treatment, no medication): -0.1190 %/yr.

Results

Category n β/yr 95% CI p-value
Conv. DM Medication 38 -0.1367 [-0.2056, -0.0678] <0.001 ***
▼ Treatment categories
Exercise 391 -0.1121 [-0.1676, -0.0566] <0.001 ***
IV Therapy 115 -0.0742 [-0.1610, +0.0125] 0.093
Berberine 105 -0.0535 [-0.1096, +0.0026] 0.061
Acupuncture / TCM 91 -0.0197 [-0.0962, +0.0568] 0.613
Sleep Hygiene 132 +0.0242 [-0.0389, +0.0872] 0.453
Stress / Mindfulness 175 +0.0395 [-0.0233, +0.1023] 0.217
Diet & Nutrition 392 +0.0438 [-0.0276, +0.1152] 0.229
Supplements & Botanicals 557 +0.0529 [-0.0704, +0.1762] 0.400
Hydrotherapy 45 +0.0822 [-0.0016, +0.1660] 0.055
Physical Therapy & Bodywork 218 +0.0872 [+0.0301, +0.1442] 0.003 **
Homeopathy 24 +0.1555 [+0.0510, +0.2601] 0.004 **

*** p<0.001   ** p<0.01   * p<0.05.   Amber row = medication (confounder). Treatment rows sorted by β. Negative β = faster HbA1c decline (improvement).

Interpretation

  • Exercise counseling (n=391) was the only treatment category to survive Bonferroni correction: β = -0.1121 %/yr (95% CI [-0.1676, -0.0566], p<0.001). Patients with documented exercise counseling declined ~0.10 percentage points per year faster than those without. This finding is consistent with the established evidence base for physical activity and glycemic control, and confirms the database captures expected clinical signals.
  • Conventional diabetes medications (n=38) showed the largest overall trajectory effect: β = -0.1367 %/yr (p<0.001), included as a confounder control so that treatment estimates are not inflated by co-occurrence with pharmaceutical therapy. Medicated patients entered care with higher mean baseline HbA1c (6.91% vs. 6.06%).
  • Physical Therapy & Bodywork, Homeopathy showed significant positive interactions (slower improvement). These are unlikely to represent treatment harm — a supplementary check confirmed these patients receive more of every other treatment category, not fewer. The most plausible explanation is treatment refractoriness: patients whose HbA1c is more resistant to initial interventions tend to accumulate more modalities over time. Hydrotherapy (p=0.042) does not survive Bonferroni correction, and the homeopathy subgroup is small (n=24). These are hypothesis-generating signals.
  • Diet/nutrition, stress/mindfulness, sleep hygiene, supplements, acupuncture, and IV therapy did not reach statistical significance. The null result for diet counseling likely reflects both the heterogeneity of dietary recommendations and the gap between documented recommendations and patient adherence, rather than an absence of dietary effects on glycemic control.

Secondary Analysis: HbA1c Trajectory by Diet Subtype (LME)

Same LME structure as the primary treatment analysis, but treatment flags are five collapsed diet subcategories derived from the subcategory field in the treatments table. Reference group: patients with no named diet subtype documented (n=-21 after overlap). Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.01. All findings are exploratory.

Model & Cohort

n=622 patients, 1,975 observations; ICC = 0.24; median follow-up 400 days. Reference slope (no diet subtype, no medication): -0.0817 %/yr. Covariates: baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication × time, clinic fixed effects.

Results

Diet Subtype n β/yr 95% CI p-value
Conv. DM Medication 26 -0.0681 [-0.1346, -0.0016] 0.045 *
▼ Diet subtype categories
Low carb / Keto 22 -0.1641 [-0.3111, -0.0171] 0.029 *
Whole foods / Mediterranean 179 -0.0460 [-0.0991, +0.0071] 0.089
Intermittent fasting 123 +0.0258 [-0.0359, +0.0875] 0.412
Elimination / Anti-inflammatory 59 +0.0301 [-0.0522, +0.1124] 0.473
General dietary guidance 260 +0.0562 [-0.0005, +0.1128] 0.052

*** p<0.001   ** p<0.01   * p<0.05.   Amber row = medication (confounder). Sorted by β. Bonferroni threshold: p = 0.01.

Interpretation

  • No diet subtype survived Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.01 for 5 simultaneous tests). All findings should be treated as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
  • Low carb / Keto (n=22) showed the largest nominally significant effect: β = -0.1641 %/yr (p=0.029), but does not survive correction and the subgroup is small. The direction is consistent with the evidence base for low-carbohydrate diets and glycemic control.
  • Whole foods / Mediterranean (n=179) trended favorably (β = -0.0460 %/yr, p=0.089) with the largest subgroup of the named diet types, suggesting this is worth examining in a larger sample.
  • General dietary guidance (n=260) showed a mildly positive trend (β = +0.0562 %/yr, p=0.052), likely reflecting that generic counseling is documented in more complex patients where no specific diet pattern has been identified — a form of clinical refractoriness rather than a diet effect.
  • Intermittent fasting and Elimination / Anti-inflammatory were essentially null. These categories have sufficient sample sizes to detect moderate effects, suggesting they are either genuinely ineffective in this cohort or that adherence to documented recommendations is too variable to detect a signal.

HbA1c – hs-CRP Regression Analysis

Elevated HbA1c and elevated hs-CRP frequently co-occur: chronic low-grade inflammation promotes insulin resistance, while hyperglycemia drives oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling. The published literature documents a consistent positive association between these two biomarkers across diverse populations. This analysis tests whether that relationship holds in our naturopathic patient cohort — serving both as a cross-validation of our dataset against established findings and as a baseline for future work examining whether naturopathic treatment patterns differentially affect glycemic control and systemic inflammation.

Multiple regression of HbA1c on log-transformed hs-CRP, adjusting for age, sex, and BMI. One observation per patient (first recorded value). Adults ≥18 with all four variables present (n=3,276). Outcome: HbA1c (%); β(log hs-CRP) represents the change in HbA1c (percentage points) per log-unit increase in hs-CRP.

Pooled model   R² = 0.100   adj. R² = 0.099

Term β SE t p-value
(Intercept) +4.5817 0.0633 72.345 <0.001 ***
log(hs-CRP) +0.0554 0.0105 5.260 <0.001 ***
Age +0.0095 0.0008 12.102 <0.001 ***
Sex (male) +0.1494 0.0205 7.299 <0.001 ***
BMI +0.0129 0.0018 7.036 <0.001 ***

Interpretation. In the pooled model (n=3,276; adj. R² = 0.099), log(hs-CRP) was a significant independent predictor of HbA1c after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI (β = 0.0554; p<0.001): each log-unit increase in hs-CRP was associated with 0.0554 percentage-point higher HbA1c. Age (β = 0.0095; p<0.001) and BMI (β = 0.0129; p<0.001) were also significant positive predictors, consistent with the known relationships between adiposity, age, and glycemic status. Males had significantly higher HbA1c than females (β = 0.1494; p<0.001). The model explains 10.0% of variance in HbA1c; the modest R² reflects the limited HbA1c range in this predominantly normoglycemic population. Overall, these findings are consistent with the published literature and confirm that our dataset captures the expected positive association between systemic inflammation and glycemic status.
